prize_parts.citation: For the conception, construction and operation of the IceCube neutrino observatory and the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, opening a new window on the cosmic-ray universe

statement.case_for: IceCube is the kind of result the Committee exists to recognise: nature supplied something nobody could have predicted in detail, namely a diffuse flux of TeV-PeV neutrinos of extragalactic origin, and a bold, decades-long experimental programme (AMANDA, then a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice) was needed to see it. The flux has been seen in several analysis channels, the 2017 TXS 0506+056 association and the later NGC 1068 and Galactic-plane results show that it points back to real astrophysical accelerators, and Mark Pearce, who knows detector-driven work well, independently ranks it first with a similar reading of maturity. The attribution is as compact as a collaboration of this size permits: Halzen as the driving scientist and Karle and Spiering in construction, instrumentation and the analyses that delivered the discovery. This is a discovery about where cosmic rays come from and about the high-energy universe, which is physics with real existential weight.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the discovery is the flux and the technique, not yet a complete picture of the sources, and that independent experimental confirmation is thinner than for the clocks or topological matter since KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD are still young. Attribution is also genuinely uncertain: DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA pioneers, and many IceCube leaders beyond the three names, have claims, and a three-person cut from a large collaboration is somewhat arbitrary. Several colleagues rank it low (Johansson 8, Olsson 7, Lindroth 6), and I should not mistake my own and the chair's first place for broad support.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first as a genuine conceptual step (magic wavelength, Lamb-Dicke regime) with record 1e-18 uncertainties and relativistic time-dilation tests, and finds IceCube possibly somewhat early because source identification is thin.
responses.response: I agree that the lattice clock is a real conceptual invention and that it is the most robustly supported entry in the opening ballots (I ranked it fifth, partly because I weigh an invention for measuring less than a discovery from nature, and because the redefinition of the second has not yet happened). But I disagree that IceCube is early. The discovery claimed is the astrophysical flux, which is secure and stable in interpretation, and the source question is the next chapter, not a condition for the first. The clock result is a measurement of the world we already knew; IceCube shows us a part of it we had not seen. I would, however, take your point seriously that a clock prize needs to be clearly distinguished from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion prize, and I regard B014 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B014 first as the clearest case of a new measurement technique opening new observations, with two clean laureates and a mature, reproduced technology, and he weighs coherence and linewidth control heavily.
responses.response: Kroll's case that two laureates is a cleaner attribution than IceCube's three, with a collaboration behind it, is fair and I accept it as the main advantage of B014. Where I differ is on what is being rewarded. The clock is a superb instrument whose full scientific payoff (geodesy, constants, a new second) is still ahead of it, whereas IceCube has already delivered a discovery. Wait for the SI redefinition and the dark-matter and constants searches to produce something, and the clock will be an even stronger case; I do not see that waiting costs it anything, while it is reasonable to ask whether the neutrino result should be recognised while the pioneers are alive and active.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) first as a theory-plus-experiment prize on a new class of quantum states, mature and arguably overdue, while acknowledging that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the 3D work lie outside the credited names.
responses.response: I share the appreciation that theory was confirmed by experiment, which is why I ranked B016 fourth. But your own caveat is the problem: the HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, which the Molenkamp experiment tested, and Fu-Kane-Mele and Hasan on three-dimensional insulators, fall outside the three names, and Johansson, Lindroth and Olsson all point at the 2016 prize on topological phases as a precedent that reduces novelty. I do not think a prize that has to leave out the proposers of the very experiment it rewards is yet clean enough to place ahead of a discovery with a compact attribution. It remains my second alternative.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as a detector-driven discovery, notes the confirmation of the diffuse flux and the TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and Galactic-plane results, and flags that the independent confirmation by other experiments is still thin and that the credit allocation is a judgement.
responses.response: I agree and take the caveat on independent confirmation seriously: confirmation so far comes from different IceCube analysis channels rather than different detectors, and KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD are not yet at the same sensitivity. I would ask the Committee to request an expert assessment on exactly this point, plus a historical note on the credit of DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA, before a final ballot, since the credited trio is a recollection-based reading that I would want the evaluations to check.

uncertainties: Fair allocation of credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the DUMAND/Baikal/AMANDA pioneers and other IceCube leaders is not settled by the supplied information.
How much independent confirmation by detectors other than IceCube the Committee requires before treating the discovery as secure.
Whether the Committee prefers the cleaner two-person lattice-clock configuration (B014), which has the broadest opening support, over a discovery with a harder attribution.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: my background is in string theory, quantum gravity and cosmology, and I have no known institutional or collaborative tie to the IceCube, optical lattice clock or topological insulator candidates or their credited names.
